Alright, I'll use Trump's policy outline from his website to give some structure to this.

The first issue is US-China trade reform. I agree, and I think many politicians and economists across the board agree, that some of Donald's grievances are well founded, namely intellectual property theft and lack of environmental standards and worker's rights constraints that the rest of developed economies have to contend with. That being said, there ends my agreement with him. On his website, his very first bullet point, and something he's talked at length about, is declaring China a currency manipulator in order to bring them to the "bargaining table." He sights the devaluation of the yuan over the past few years as having a deleterious affect on the cost of imported products, trade balance, and U.S. manufacturing. These three points are all mostly unfounded, and what averse affects that this supposed manipulation has brought on the U.S. is neither appreciable nor principle to either the rising deficit or loss of manufacturing - the cost of imported products or rising cost point being irrelevant here, as it is attributable to variables external to his main point. Starting with his premise of currency manipulation, in order that we declare China a currency manipulator we would have to, in good faith, declare all countries who use a central banking model as currency manipulators being that the monetary policy that China engages in is on par with regulatory standards of all central banking authorities. To further my point of this being a non-issue, real exchange rates on currency, where he supposes manipulation is occurring, factor almost negligibly into job creation or loss and the price of imports. The increase in the price of goods can be explained by nominal exchange rates that have, admittedly, in the last twenty or so years, gone against the American market, but that is to be expected and was not unforeseen considering that the Chinese economy is an emerging market that has grown vastly in that time period. The increase in import prices that we see can be explained by that; that as an economy grows, so too it's costs, thus increasing the price at the nominal exchange rate to import from said country. To the point of the trade deficits, this is calculated by nominal rates and thus has little to do with currency regulation. Now, as far as loss of manufacturing jobs is concerned, this absolutely has nothing to do with currencies. With the advent of globalization and free trade, we've opened what were once closed labor markets and integrated them into international labor markets where, because of the higher relative cost of living in the US, American workers are being out priced by their international competitors. Though much of our manufactured product comes out of China, it's not exclusively so and there are many countries that American companies have outsourced labor to.

While US-China trade relations are one of my biggest issues with Trump's economic plans, it's not the only one. I take issue with his domestic tax plan that includes reducing corporate tax as a means to keep companies in America, increase profit and the tax base, and create new manufacturing jobs. While lower taxes may help to prevent corporate inversion, I see no way in which the other two points could be achieved by such a singular policy change. The idea of trickle down economics worked well under Reagan for precisely the reason that it won't now - free trade. Under Reagan there was no or very limited free trade and consequently, lowering taxes on corporations freed up capital that, for corporations, was financially advantageous to reinvest in the American economy, thus creating jobs, increasing the tax base, so on and so forth. But now that American is trading freely with most of the developed world, I go back to my statement about competition and international labor markets in that, should the corporate tax rate be reduced, the aggregate corporate savings of all companies big and small would be reinvested by and large in globalized economic business models that don't necessarily entail a priority placed on American investment and domestic job creation but rather, wherever profits can be maximized. Another tenet of the Reagan economic model is that lower corporate taxes help small business, and while this is true and remains true today, it also exacerbates one problem and completely ignores another. Firstly, that lower tax rates on all businesses is disproportionately advantageous to large companies whose tax windfall would free up much more capital to further reinvest and drive prices lower and, considering economies of scale, makes competition that much more difficult for small businesses. The problem ignored is that because of the loss of jobs and stagnant wages, the capital required to open a small business is growing further out of reach, and while a lower corporate tax may help small business in some respect, it does nothing to encourage an increase in number of small business. Neither of these two situations increase the tax base where it is needed per se, nor does the tax savings on large companies encourage domestic job creation per se. While the tax base as a whole would increase with lower corporate tax, the increase would come from taxable revenue generated by large corporations and not because middle and lower class jobs were being created or their wages increasing. To conclude my thoughts on this particular issue, there are some numbers that Trump has outlined in changing the tax code as a whole, and while they are too broad for any kind of thorough analysis, on the surface, it appears to be a net decrease in overall tax income. While it is not a necessarily a negative policy stance, it becomes one when predicated on reduced taxes generating more wealth for the middle and lower class, as discussed above.

To his points on immigration reform, central to Trump's policy, a wall between Mexico and the United States, which will be paid for by Mexico. The entirety of his position is, essentially, that by outlawing remittance from illegal aliens in the United States to recipients in Mexico, Mexicans and the Mexican government will protest because of the reliance of Mexican families on remittance from illegals working in the United States. In essence, strong arming them to pay for the wall in exchange for something that, frankly, I'm not entirely certain of. His argument is circular. His end goal is to end illegal immigration to the United States, thus ending remittances by illegal aliens, by means of denying current illegal aliens remittance in order to pressure the Mexican people into paying for a wall that will end illegal immigration, in exchange for not ending illegal remittance that they won't then be receiving by virtue of there being no illegal immigrants. But to suppose for a moment, that this wall were to be built, we come to review of history and what we know of wall building. In the history of mankind, walls have existed merely as a deterrent and have time and time again failed in the presence of those determined enough surmount them; from the Mongols that poured through the Great Wall of China to the thousands of defects that escaped over the Berlin Wall. Quite truthfully, human history doesn't bode well for the efficacy of walls as cure all, and that diplomacy, public policy, and economy seem much more suitable for stable, long term solutions. In terms of finances, it seems to be overlooked that it's initial cost to be built isn't the largest cost and would be minimal in comparison to the costs of manning, maintaining, and supplying it. If we were to even attempt it, these things would be absolutely necessary in order that we may see some degree of usefulness for it. A hypothetical wall aside, It's plainly apparent that the illegal immigration in the United States is not largely because of a lack of boarder security but a lack of properly policed current immigration laws. It's well document that the majority of illegal immigrants are the product of over extended visas. Trump does go on to propose reforms to immigration laws but speaks nothing to how we go about enforcing them or how the costs might be paid for. It seems to me, again, that his solution is more or less singular, i.e. build a wall. Moving on, Trump goes on to say, he would like to level a tariff at Mexico as well, that the Mexican government is taking advantage of the United States with trade subsidies, and that import cost increases caused by the tariff would be offset by the gains and jobs it would create in the economy. Again, I reference my previous comments in regards to labor markets. Further on, he says that Mexico is in much more need of our market that we of theirs, but that it's a difficult assessment to make considering that Mexico ranks third among countries we import from and third among countries we export to.

In conclusion I will say this, I agree, for the most part, with Mr. Trump's assessment of what is ailing the American economy right now, but as I've illustrated, I have some very deep concerns with the way he intends to go about addressing them.
